  ⎿  #!/bin/sh
  ⎿  # Fetch models and test data into the layout the code expects (see SETUP.md); verifies sha256.
  ⎿  # Run from the repo root. Needs: curl, tar, sha256sum, gh (logged in; IndicTrans2 is a private release asset).
  ⎿  set -eu
  ⎿  ROOT=$(pwd)
  ⎿  PARENT=$(dirname "$ROOT")
  ⎿  HF=https://huggingface.co
  ⎿  
  ⎿  get() {  # url dest sha256
  ⎿    if [ -f "$2" ] && echo "$3  $2" | sha256sum -c --status; then echo "ok   $2"; return; fi
  ⎿    mkdir -p "$(dirname "$2")"
  ⎿    curl -fL --retry 3 -o "$2.part" "$1" && mv "$2.part" "$2"
  ⎿    echo "$3  $2" | sha256sum -c
  ⎿  }
  ⎿  
  ⎿  get "$HF/nvidia/stt_en_fastconformer_hybrid_large_streaming_multi/resolve/main/stt_en_fastconformer_hybrid_large_streaming_multi.nemo" \
  ⎿    "$PARENT/models/fastconformer_114m.nemo" 8db5289d5238aca839b84f5afdd66eb1aa64413feb9c2a915940b291012aff8b
  ⎿  P=$HF/rhasspy/piper-voices/resolve/main/hi/hi_IN/rohan/medium
  ⎿  get "$P/hi_IN-rohan-medium.onnx" models/piper/hi_IN-rohan-medium.onnx \
  ⎿    b65dc80fb34d9dcd1cf684cb297966a34983bbc93bb1696fe207f32b0b33a091
  ⎿  get "$P/hi_IN-rohan-medium.onnx.json" models/piper/hi_IN-rohan-medium.onnx.json \
  ⎿    07b9ae19bd0bac7fbbc99f7ee69c91245eb5470e926632c31fc0c50ba653c817
  ⎿  
  ⎿  # IndicTrans2 en-hi dist-200M int8 ONNX: custom export (VoiceAI edge/export_indictrans2), hosted as a release asset.
  ⎿  MT=models/indictrans2-en-hi-onnx
  ⎿  if [ ! -f "$MT/encoder.int8.onnx" ]; then
  ⎿    gh release download assets-v1 --repo Krishnag1729/Voicemesh --pattern 'indictrans2-en-hi-int8.tar.gz' --dir /tmp --clobber
  ⎿    mkdir -p "$MT" && tar -xzf /tmp/indictrans2-en-hi-int8.tar.gz -C "$MT"
  ⎿  fi
  ⎿  (cd "$MT" && sha256sum -c "$ROOT/scripts/indictrans2.sha256")
  ⎿  
  ⎿  if [ ! -d "$PARENT/data_ext/LibriSpeech/test-clean" ]; then
  ⎿    mkdir -p "$PARENT/data_ext"
  ⎿    curl -fL --retry 3 https://www.openslr.org/resources/12/test-clean.tar.gz | tar -xz -C "$PARENT/data_ext"
  ⎿  fi
  ⎿  echo "assets ready"
  ⎿  model.SRC: OK
  ⎿  model.TGT: OK
  ⎿  encoder.int8.onnx: OK
  ⎿  decoder.int8.onnx: OK

  ⎿  | E4 | EDF scheduling equals FCFS | engine repo (SPEC §3): FCFS = EDF at 112 streams | holds; not re-tested here |
  ⎿  | E6 | gate saves bytes, maybe not radio energy | gate sends 45 % of chunks; radio energy needs a real phone | bytes: holds; energy: open |
  ⎿  | P1 | TTS fits on CPU | r = 0.092 core-s per audio-s at 8 processes | holds; TTS sets capacity |
  ⎿  
  ⎿  ## 9. Limits and open items
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - Long turns: last clause starts 8.3 s (p95) after the speaker stops; faster TTS or shorter commit pauses would cut it.
  ⎿  - After a node loss the replayed ≤6 s is re-transcribed, so up to 6 s of Hindi may repeat.
  ⎿  - No human Hindi reference: E2 measures agreement, not adequacy.
  ⎿  - CPU power is a util model (RAPL unreadable); prices are assumptions passed as flags to `bench.cost`.
  ⎿  - Not yet done: radio energy and memory on a real 2 GB phone, one-hour soak, voice licences, capacity at ~60 % pauses.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  ## 10. Viva notes
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **Why is the phone thin?** A 2 GB phone cannot hold ASR + MT + TTS; it only gates, Opus-encodes and plays back, at 88 MB PSS.
  ⎿  - **What limits capacity?** Hindi TTS on CPU at 70 users; ASR on a 6 GB laptop-class GPU runs at 0.31 utilisation there.
  ⎿  - **Why clauses, not sentences?** Speech starts before the speaker finishes: turn first audio p50 is 0.36 s. The cost is wording drift (chrF++ 68.7 vs sentence translation).
  ⎿  - **Does the silence gate hurt accuracy?** WER +0.47 pp (4.02 → 4.49 %), inside the 0.5 pp gate, and it sends only 45 % of chunks.
  ⎿  - **What happens if a GPU node dies?** Sessions move to a live node and resume from the 6 s Opus replay buffer; 4/4 resumed.
  ⎿  - **What does it cost?** $0.0037 per user-hour on the lab PC including the cloud gateway; cloud_t4@0.54 $0.016, cloud_t4@0.2 $0.0062.
  ⎿  - **Why does measured capacity differ from the model?** The model predicted ~87 users from mean TTS load; bursts of clauses push the tail over 2 s first, so 70 passes repeatedly.

⏺ The 8.3 s tail comes from audio queueing up for playback, not from slow processing:
- The server takes 1.2 s (p95) per clause from end of speech to first audio.
- Hindi audio runs 1.27× as long as the English, so each clause waits for the earlier ones to finish playing.

The e2e bench is now running in the background at rates 1.0, 1.15 and 1.3; each run streams about 4 minutes of audio in real time, so it takes roughly 12 minutes. `results/` is backed up, and I'll restore it before reporting. Faster Hindi may be harder to understand, so you'll choose the default rate.

till what cost are we at and how many users we can cater per GPU simultaneously currently?
Response (17 lines) — click to expand
⏺ **At TTS rate 1.15, one lab GPU box serves 80 users at once, at $0.0034 per user-hour.**

**Users per GPU:**
- **Lab PC (RTX 3050 + i9-12900K):** 80 at once (p95 1.74 s); 85 fails. The CPU running Hindi TTS (8 processes) is the limit, not the GPU.
- **The GPU itself:** ASR is only 0.35 busy at 80 users. Extrapolating from the M6 load runs, ASR alone would handle about 230 users, so the GPU could serve roughly 3× more if TTS had more CPU.

**Cost per user-hour at 80 users (lab):** $0.0034, about $0.27/h for all 80.
- Hardware: $0.00214 (a $1500 PC over 3 years at 8 h/day).
- Network egress: $0.00083.
- Cloud gateway VM: $0.00025.
- Electricity: $0.00017 (139 W at $0.10/kWh).

**Cloud T4 with 4 vCPU:** about 40 users, since TTS scales with cores.
- On-demand ($0.54/h): $0.014 per user-hour.
- Spot ($0.20/h): $0.0055 per user-hour.

Caveats: CPU power is estimated from utilisation because the energy counter is unreadable, prices are assumed values passed to `bench.cost`, and 80 users hasn't had a 1 h soak yet (that ran at 70).

so what number of GPU's (Assume Datacenter based GPU's not RTX 3050) would be required on a datacentre if we want to run this for say 100000 users simultaneously? and what will be the cost to us in paise per second?
Response (21 lines) — click to expand
⏺ **About 35–240 datacentre GPUs, depending on the card. Cost comes to roughly ₹10–23 per second (≈1,000–2,250 paise/s), and CPUs for TTS make up most of it, not GPUs.** These are extrapolations from the lab numbers at 80 users. Nothing has been measured on a datacentre GPU, and prices and ₹88/$ are my assumptions.

**What scales with users (measured, plus 15% headroom for peaks):**
- **Hindi TTS (CPU):** 10 users per core, so about 10,000 vCPU.
- **Translation (CPU):** about 0.027 cores per user, so about 4,000 vCPU.
- **Gateway and Opus audio:** about 1,000 vCPU. Total is about 17,000 vCPU.
- **ASR (GPU):** the RTX 3050 handles about 160 users safely. Scaling by GPU speed gives about 200 L4s, about 70–90 A100s, or about 36–48 H100s.

**Cost for 100,000 users at once:**

| Pricing | $/h | ₹/s | paise/s | paise per user-second |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| On-demand (vCPU $0.04, L4 $0.80) | ~920 | ~22.5 | **~2,250** | 0.023 |
| Spot/committed (vCPU $0.015, L4 $0.35) | ~400 | ~9.9 | **~990** | 0.010 |
| Today's cost model (2,500 T4 boxes, 40 users each) | 1,400 | 34 | 3,420 | 0.034 |

The T4-box model overpays because each GPU sits mostly idle. Egress (~$53/h) and the gateway (~$25/h) are included in every row.

**Biggest lever:** move TTS (and translation) onto the GPU. The CPU fleet shrinks and the GPU count becomes the real cost driver. This is unmeasured and would be the next experiment.

⏺ Yes, mostly. At 80 users on the lab PC, ASR is the only stage on the GPU, and it's busy about 35% of the time:
- **Busy time:** each 160 ms audio chunk takes 55 ms to process for all 80 users together (p95 82 ms), so the GPU waits about 65% of the time.
- **Power:** the board draws 34 W, against 11 W idle and a 70 W limit for the 6 GB RTX 3050.
- **Where the load is:** the CPU is the bottleneck. TTS is 57% busy and translation 54%, and those are the levels where latency starts to break.

That 35% is wall-clock time of the ASR step, which includes some CPU-side work, so the GPU kernels are busy even less.

So the GPU has room for about 3× more users, but the CPU that runs TTS and translation runs out first. In a datacentre this gets worse, because a faster GPU sits idle even longer while the cores do the expensive work.

Putting TTS (Piper is an ONNX model) and translation (CTranslate2 supports CUDA) on that idle GPU would rebalance it. That would be the next experiment, measured with `bench.load`.
Turn 27#
so if we somehow able to make GPU's more use we can make this system more effecient?
Response (17 lines) — click to expand
⏺ Yes, most likely. Right now the CPU caps capacity while the GPU is about 65% idle. If translation and TTS ran on the GPU, capacity would be set by the GPU, which has room for about 3× more users on this PC.

**What it could gain (estimates, not measured):**
- **Lab PC:** about 150–230 users instead of 80, so cost per user drops roughly 2–3×.
- **Datacentre:** most of the ~14,000 vCPU for TTS and translation goes away, and cost then tracks GPU count. Big GPUs batch many users at once, which is where they are cheapest per user.

**What could go wrong:**
- **ASR deadlines:** ASR must finish each 160 ms chunk on time. TTS and translation on the same GPU could delay it, so ASR needs priority, for example separate CUDA streams with a deadline-miss check.
- **Batching:** the GPU only pays off if TTS calls from many users are batched together. Piper's API synthesises one sentence at a time, so batching may need a custom ONNX runner.
- **Memory:** the 6 GB card holds ASR at 1.85 GB, so translation and TTS should fit, but that is unverified.

**Suggested order, each step measured with `bench.load`:**
1. Translation on the GPU (CTranslate2 `device="cuda"`), the easy one.
2. Piper TTS on the CUDA execution provider.
3. Batch TTS across users if step 2 alone doesn't pay off.

Shall I add this to PLAN as M16 and start with step 1?

  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **Non-autoregressive vs. autoregressive:** A GPU-incremental TTS paper batches requests that arrive within a short window, but new requests must wait for the next round, which is the scheduling tradeoff to watch. For the non-incremental twin, the TTS requests received over a short period are constructed into a batch for inference. New requests received during the current round need to wait in the queue for the next round to be processed.
  ⎿  - **Batching trades per-stream speed for aggregate throughput:** A pure-C engine's CUDA and Metal backends report that in batch mode each step does the work of B slots, so per-request RTF rises. Its M2 Pro measurements show per-request RTF rising from 1.01 at one request to 1.44 at four, with throughput speed-up of 2.81× at four requests. Server request-batching on both (plus CPU): ~2.8× throughput on Metal, ~3.35× on CUDA.
  ⎿  - **Concurrency numbers for a TTS model:** Voxtral TTS on a single H200 scaled from concurrency 1 to 32, with throughput rising from 119 to 1,431 characters per second per GPU while per-request RTF reached 0.302 at concurrency 32. For Orpheus, one report says a baseline of about 24 concurrent real-time connections per H100 rose to 216 after system-level optimization.
  ⎿  - **Batching limits for streaming:** A faster IndexTTS-2 study found that gains diminishing beyond batch size 8, and that streaming TTFA increases with batch size, making large-batch streaming impractical for latency-sensitive scenarios.
  ⎿  - **Vocoder/decoder batching:** One TTS deployment guide suggests dynamic batching with a short timeout (e.g., 15 milliseconds) for the audio decoder, and notes that in-flight batching is not possible for the audio decoder.

  ⎿  - **REEF (OSDI 2022):** The paper describes a GPU inference serving system that enables microsecond-scale kernel preemption. It preempts best-effort kernels by resetting them, and it pads real-time kernels with best-effort kernels to use idle GPU capacity. The authors report under 2% end-to-end latency overhead for real-time tasks and up to 7.7× higher throughput compared with dedicating the GPU to real-time tasks. This paper presents REEF, the first GPU-accelerated DNN inference serving system that enables microsecond-scale kernel preemption and controlled concurrent execution in GPU scheduling. The padding mechanism dynamically pads the real-time kernel with appropriate best-effort kernels to fully utilize the GPU with negligible overhead.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **Orion (EuroSys 2024):** Orion intercepts kernel launches from multiple clients on a shared GPU and schedules at the operator level, accounting for each operator's compute and memory needs. The authors integrate it with PyTorch. Orion significantly improves tail latency compared to state-of-the-art baselines for a high-priority inference job while collocating best-effort inference jobs to increase per-GPU request throughput by up to 7.3x.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **Classification conflict:** Orion is cited as a spatial-sharing system in one source, while REEF is labeled temporal sharing. A later paper (Hummingbird, arXiv 2601.04071) groups spatial sharing [MIG, multi_stream, Zico@ATC21, orion@eurosys24] and temporal sharing [REEF, TGS@NSDI23, tally]. The REEF paper itself frames the work around preemption, so the spatial/temporal labels depend on the source. The same Hummingbird paper says the spatial sharing techniques can hardly provide SLO guarantees due to severe interference.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **Related work:** Hummingbird (arXiv 2601.04071) proposes microsecond-scale GPU preemption for SLO-oriented sharing. Deft (MICRO 2025) targets preemption delay on edge GPUs by inserting kernel synchronization points. It reports reduces inference delay and SLO violations by 28% and 14% respectively relative to state-of-the-art GPU sharing schemes. Fico is a poster-level proposal that compares against REEF, KRISP, and Orion, and reports inference latency by 37.3% on average compared to prior methods.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  I ran one search, so these are the highlights rather than a full survey. For verification, the REEF and Orion details come from the USENIX and hgpu/EuroSys pages, and the Hummingbird and Deft claims are from arXiv and IBM Research abstracts.

  ⎿  The paper's approach has two main parts. It constrains both the look-ahead and past contexts in the encoder, and introduces an activation caching mechanism so the non-autoregressive encoder can operate autoregressively during inference. The caching removes the need for any buffer or overlapping chunks, avoiding unnecessary duplicate computation. The authors also say the design aims to eliminate the accuracy gap between training and inference time, which is common in many streaming models. The encoder works with CTC and RNN-Transducer (RNNT) decoders, and the authors used FastConformer for experiments because it is more than 2X faster than Conformer.

  ⎿  I didn't find a single peer-reviewed paper that compares MPS, MIG, and time-slicing on inference throughput and latency. The closest sources are vendor and practitioner benchmarks, and they point in different directions.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **NVIDIA's voice-AI pipeline benchmark (A100, Kubernetes):** MIG achieved approximately 1.00 requests per second per GPU compared to 0.76 req/s for time-slicing configurations. Time-slicing had lower latency for bursty TTS work, 144.7ms mean TTS latency versus MIG's 168.2ms. NVIDIA's own write-up is the primary source here, MIG (hardware): Highest efficiency.
  ⎿  - **KubeCon NA 2024 talk (Klues and Chen), as photographed by a blogger:** Throughput stayed at about 100 req/s with and without sharing for both time-slicing and MPS. MPS latency rose slightly, from about 4312 to 4475 microseconds, while time-slicing stayed roughly flat. The blogger notes the numbers are indicative because the chart text is small. For MPS it lists improved utilisation, no performance degradation and low overhead, with caveats: limited fault isolation, slower startup.
  ⎿  - **Pebble LLM benchmark (via an aggregator):** MPS sharing costs roughly 7.5% output throughput and adds ~19.5% to time-per-output-token (TPOT) latency versus a dedicated GPU, while cutting GPU cost in half. I could not verify this against the original Pebble source.
  ⎿  - **Broadcom/VMware (vGPU, not bare metal):** Time-sliced vGPU lets a VM use the full GPU during its slice, while MIG caps each workload at its partition. Neighbor's idle cycles: Scheduler reallocates unused slices (time-sliced) vs. idle cycles stranded in partition (MIG).
  ⎿  - **A 2026 arXiv study:** A secondary source cites it as showing up to 30% better performance and about 20% lower energy, but also about 30% worse performance under memory contention. I did not retrieve the arXiv paper itself, so treat this as unverified.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  Overall, the results depend on workload. MIG tends to win on throughput under heavy mixed load and offers fault isolation. Time-slicing can be better for bursty, latency-sensitive requests and has less startup overhead. MPS adds small throughput and latency costs but allows more sharing. For a citable paper, search arXiv or the KubeCon NA 2024 session materials directly, and check the 2026 arXiv study's title, which I could not confirm.

  ⎿  
  ⎿  **Orca (OSDI 2022)**
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - The paper's core idea is iteration-level scheduling, which makes the scheduler decide at every model iteration rather than per request. Its authors say this lets finished requests leave early and new arrivals join without waiting for the whole batch to drain.
  ⎿  - The paper pairs this with selective batching, which batches only certain operations in a Transformer. The authors report 36.9× throughput over FasterTransformer at the same latency on GPT-3 175B.
  ⎿  - The term "continuous batching" is used in later sources for the same technique. One source notes that the research literature follows Orca in calling it iteration-level scheduling.
  ⎿  - FriendliAI, a co-author's company, says iteration batching is protected by patents in the US and Korea.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  **vLLM / PagedAttention (SOSP 2023)**
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - The paper's authors identify internal fragmentation, external fragmentation, and poor cross-request sharing as the main sources of KV-cache waste in existing systems.
  ⎿  - PagedAttention borrows the OS virtual-memory paging idea so the KV cache can live in non-contiguous, fixed-size blocks. The arXiv abstract says this drives waste close to zero.
  ⎿  - The paper reports 2–4× throughput gains over FasterTransformer and Orca at the same latency.
  ⎿  - Some secondary blog posts cite a 24× figure and sub-4% waste. Those numbers don't match the paper's 2–4× claim, so I'd treat them with caution.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  **Caveats:** Several results came from blogs, a Scribd upload, and a course slide deck rather than the proceedings. For citations, check the USENIX OSDI '22 page for Orca and the ACM DOI (10.1145/3600006.3613165) or arXiv:2309.06180 for vLLM.
  ⎿

  ⎿  
  ⎿  **Cascade architecture and latency**
  ⎿  - The SimulU paper (2026) evaluates streaming cascades on MuST-C v1 tst-COMMON. Latency is set by the cut-off frame for StreamAtt-based cascades and by speech segment size for LA-based ones. It reports a start offset of roughly 1–2 seconds for its own system in most language pairs, and it cites about 2 seconds as a rough limit for ear-voice span. [arxiv.org/pdf/2603.16924]
  ⎿  - The same paper found that swapping the TTS component to SeamlessM4T's TTS sharply degraded ASR-BLEU, which suggests TTS choice is a major quality factor in cascades. [arxiv.org/pdf/2603.16924]
  ⎿  - The HW-TSC IWSLT 2023 system describes the standard cascade: a streaming ASR module, a streaming text MT module, and an offline TTS module. [aclweb.org/anthology/2023.iwslt-1.36.pdf]
  ⎿  - A 2022 MLLP-VRAIN IWSLT entry used streaming-ready ASR, MT, and TTS for English-to-German, with decoding tuned for streaming inference. [mllp.upv.es]
  ⎿  
  ⎿  **StreamSpeech**
  ⎿  - StreamSpeech is a direct simultaneous S2ST model trained with multi-task learning. It can run offline and simultaneous ASR, speech translation, and speech synthesis in one model. [arxiv.org/pdf/2406.03049v1]
  ⎿  - It was evaluated on CVSS, where it reported state-of-the-art results for both offline S2ST and simultaneous S2ST. It can also show intermediate ASR or translation text during simultaneous output. [arxiv.org/pdf/2406.03049v1]
  ⎿  
  ⎿  **Latency and trade-offs (vendor sources, treat with caution)**
  ⎿  - A Deepgram blog reports that TTS alone accounted for an RTF of 0.64 out of a total 1.04 in one cascade benchmark on an A100 (Whisper-medium, MADLAD-400, CosyVoice 2).   ⎿  - A Forasoft guide describes SeamlessM4T v2 as sub-second end-to-end but weaker on long technical sentences, and says cascades are preferred for quality. These are marketing-oriented claims without published methodology. [forasoft.com/learn/real-time-speech-translation-live-video]

  ⎿  - I found no results with head-to-head SeamlessStreaming numbers against StreamSpeech or a cascade on the same benchmark. For that, look at the SeamlessStreaming paper from Meta and any papers that compare against StreamSpeech on CVSS, plus the SimulU paper's tables.

  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **Label-looping algorithm (arXiv 2406.06220):** Label-looping is an algorithmic speedup that can be stacked with other optimizations. At batch size 32, adding CUDA graphs raised full-pipeline RTFx from 751.2 to 1232.7 for RNN-T and from 1006.8 to 1393.4 for TDT. Non-encoder RTFx for TDT rose from 2634.2 to 9614.8. The paper notes TorchScript and CUDA graphs are not compatible, so they were not combined. The speedup reported from all other tables is solely from the algorithmic changes of the label-looping algorithm.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **Galvez, Bataev, Xu, Kaldewey (Interspeech 2024, arXiv 2406.03791):** This paper uses CUDA 12.4 graph conditional nodes for exact greedy decoding. It reports a 2.5x end-to-end speedup for a 1.1 billion parameter RNN-T model. Applied to label-looping, it reports 1.7x and 1.4x end-to-end speedups for RNN-T and TDT models respectively. The label-looping version was also described as up to 2.0X faster than conventional batched decoding when using batch size 32.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **NVIDIA NeMo blog:** This post covers the same combination of bfloat16 autocasting, label-looping, and CUDA Graphs, which it says boosted the inference speed of NeMo ASR models by up to 10x. The blog's headline figure is a cumulative result across all those changes, not the label-looping gain alone.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **WIND (arXiv 2505.13765):** This later paper applies CUDA graphs to label-looping batched inference and reports that CUDA-graph optimization brings significant speedup for inference in all cases.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  Caveat: the 2.0x, 1.7x, and 1.4x figures come from the search snippets, not the full papers, and they are measured on the authors' own hardware and setups. The RTFx table comes from the label-looping paper's full text and is also specific to its benchmark setup. I did not confirm the author list for the label-looping paper from these results.

  ⎿  The search didn't turn up anything on batching or padding for VITS or Piper, so the answer to that part is not in these results. It did surface a few relevant points on CUDA speed.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **Piper CUDA shows a speedup when the CPU fallback is fixed.** In a Piper pull request, one user's CUDA run dropped from about 29.6 seconds to 3.0 seconds (model load included) after a patch. The same ONNX Runtime warning about nodes not landing on the preferred provider, with shape ops moved to CPU, appears in the logs ([github.com/rhasspy/piper/pull/172](https://github.com/rhasspy/piper/pull/172)).
  ⎿  - **Piper's GPU flag is wired to a single provider.** An issue shows Piper's `load` function picks either CUDA or CPU, with no other GPU provider option. Its author patched it to use a different provider for inference ([github.com/rhasspy/piper/issues/483](https://github.com/rhasspy/piper/issues/483)).
  ⎿  - **CUDA graphs need fixed input shapes.** A community API reference notes that CUDA graphs speed up execution only with fixed input shapes ([www.mintlify.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/api/python/providers](https://www.mintlify.com/microsoft/onnxruntime/api/python/providers)). That matters for variable-length VITS input: padding to fixed buckets would be the usual way to make it usable, but I found no source confirming this for VITS.
  ⎿  - **CUDA speed can disappoint on small models.** A developer testing a tiny MatMul model found the CPU faster than CUDA, and the thread attributes this to environment and setup issues ([forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/onnx-runtime-gpu/327411](https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/onnx-runtime-gpu/327411)).
  ⎿  
  ⎿  For the batching and padding question, the next step would be the Piper or VITS repository issues, or the ONNX Runtime CUDA EP documentation on dynamic shapes.

  ⎿  
  ⎿  I found four relevant papers. None is an exact match for "EDF on a GPU edge server," but DeepRT and EdgeServing are the closest.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  1. **EdgeServing: Deadline-Aware Multi-DNN Serving at the Edge** (arXiv 2605.05527). This is the most recent and closest match. It targets several DNN models sharing one edge GPU. It uses time-division GPU sharing with early-exit inference and a "stability score" to choose the model, exit point, and batch size. Its reported results are lower SLO violation ratios and P95 latency than baselines.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  2. **DeepRT: A Soft Real Time Scheduler for Computer Vision Applications on the Edge** (arXiv 2105.01803, 2021). This is a multi-tenant edge GPU scheduler for soft real-time requests. Its DisBatcher batches requests while providing latency guarantees for requests that pass an admission control module. It also has an adaptation module for overruns.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  3. **Towards Fair and Firm Real-Time Scheduling in DNN Multi-Tenant Multi-Accelerator Systems via Reinforcement Learning** (arXiv 2403.00766). This paper uses deep reinforcement learning to meet per-tenant deadline hit-rate targets across heterogeneous accelerators. Its baselines include EDF combined with a spatial allocation heuristic (EDF-H), so it is useful as an EDF comparison point.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  4. **DARIS** (arXiv 2504.08795). This is a real-time multi-tenant DNN scheduler for GPU partitions. It reports higher throughput than batching and other schedulers, and high-priority tasks meeting deadlines.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  A fifth result, **Split-Gate Pooled-Evidence Stochastic-Rollout Scheduling** (arXiv 2608.08338), addresses multi-tenant edge inference with a shared wireless uplink feeding a GPU server. It is relevant if your setting includes network transmission, not just GPU execution.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  For EDF specifically, the RL paper's EDF-H baseline and DeepRT's admission control are the most direct starting points. I have not checked the full text of any of these papers, so the details above come from search snippets and abstracts.

  ⎿  
  ⎿  The paper is Nexus: A GPU Cluster Engine for Accelerating DNN-Based Video Analysis, published at SOSP '19 (October 2019). Its authors are from the University of Washington, Microsoft Research, AWS, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and Northeastern University.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **Problem and approach:** The paper addresses serving DNNs across a GPU cluster, and it argues that GPUs need sustained high utilization to be cost-effective. Its approach combines cluster-scale scheduling, co-scheduling of related DNN invocations, and executing DNN fragments rather than whole models. ([microsoft.com research page](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/nexus-a-gpu-cluster-engine-for-accelerating-dnn-based-video-analysis/))
  ⎿  - **Results:** On 16 GPUs, the authors report Nexus handling 1.8 to 12.7 times the request rate of state-of-the-art systems while keeping latency within bounds at least 99% of the time. On a 100-GPU cluster, a multi-application deployment violated latency SLOs on 0.27% of requests. ([same source](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/nexus-a-gpu-cluster-engine-for-accelerating-dnn-based-video-analysis/))
  ⎿  - **Squishy bin packing:** Nexus's scheduler is described as a batching-aware approach that does bin packing with variable-size bins, deciding the number of GPUs, the placement of DNNs, and execution order. ([Notes summarizing the paper](https://yuchu.notion.site/Nexus-A-GPU-Cluster-for-Accelerating-Neural-Networks-for-Video-Analysis-de1a843693c94085bd598ca1da1bf2b4)) Course notes also list squishy bin packing alongside adaptive batching and breakdown of latency SLOs for complex queries. ([CS744 notes](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~shivaram/cs744-fa21-slides/cs744-nexus-notes.pdf))
  ⎿  - **Batching and query scheduling:** The system lets users group related DNN calls as queries with a query-level latency SLO, and automatically assigns batch sizes. It can also batch shared portions of networks, which matters because transfer learning makes models nearly identical. ([Notes](https://yuchu.notion.site/Nexus-A-GPU-Cluster-for-Accelerating-Neural-Networks-for-Video-Analysis-de1a843693c94085bd598ca1da1bf2b4))
  ⎿  - **Code:** The open-source implementation is at github.com/uwsampl/nexus, and the project describes itself as a scalable serving system for DNN applications on GPU clusters. ([GitHub](https://github.com/uwsampl/nexus))
  ⎿  
  ⎿  The full paper PDF is available from the Microsoft Research and University of Washington pages if you want the detailed evaluation.

  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **CPU:** CTranslate2 3.6.0 at int8 reached 860.2 tokens per second on the OpenNMT-py WMT14 model, with 529MB max memory and 26.78 BLEU. The CPU runs used 4 threads on a c5.2xlarge Amazon EC2 instance equipped with an Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8275CL CPU.
  ⎿  - **GPU:** On the same model family, CTranslate2 3.6.0 at int8 reached 8567.2 tokens per second, with 1005MB GPU memory. The GPU hardware isn't identified in the snippets I saw.
  ⎿  - **Rough ratio:** About 10x in favor of GPU int8 (8567 vs 860), with the caveat that the two rows may not have been run on identical setups.

First, the project says the results presented below are only valid for the configuration used during this benchmark: absolute and relative performance may change with different settings. Second, the GPU int8 row is not a clean batch-size experiment. A third-party fork of the README says translations are running beam search with a size of 4 and a maximum batch size of 32 unless otherwise noted, but I didn't find batch-size sweeps.

  ⎿  Web search results for query: "CUDA stream priorities concurrent kernel execution latency-critical inference interference study"
  ⎿  
  ⎿  Links: [{"title":"iGniter: Interference-Aware GPU Resource Provisioning for Predictable DNN Inference in the Cloud","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.01713"},{"title":"Strait: Perceiving Priority and Interference in ML Inference Serving","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.28175"},{"title":"ML Inference Scheduling with Predictable Latency","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.18725"},{"title":"arxiv.org","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04848v1"},{"title":"ccbp taco18 final","url":"https://hzhou.wordpress.ncsu.edu/files/2022/12/ccbp_taco18_final.pdf"},{"title":"par.nsf.gov","url":"https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10385875"},{"title":"Interference analysis of shared last-level cache on embedded GP-GPUs with multiple CUDA streams","url":"https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2310.04848"},{"title":"Extended Abstract Characterizing Concurrency0AMechanisms for NVIDIA GPUs under Deep Learning0AWorkloads","url":"https://www.performance2021.deib.polimi.it/www.performance2021.deib.polimi.it/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/Extended-Abstract-Characterizing-Concurrency0AMechanisms-for-NVIDIA-GPUs-under-Deep-Learning0AWorkloads.pdf"},{"title":"osdi22 han","url":"https://www.usenix.net/system/files/osdi22-han.pdf"},{"title":"DS1 spectrogram: Strait: Perceiving Priority and Interference in ML Inference Serving","url":"https://tldr.takara.ai/p/2604.28175"}]
  ⎿  
  ⎿  The search turned up several relevant studies. The most direct evidence is about stream priorities failing to protect inference latency.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **Priority streams don't preempt running work.** A workshop abstract on NVIDIA GPUs under deep learning workloads reports that priority streams led to high and less predictable turnaround times for inference tasks, mainly because the mechanism cannot preempt executing thread blocks of the training task. It describes a "compounded delay" effect where high-priority kernels wait behind lower-priority blocks that are already running (its thread blocks take precedence only over unscheduled blocks of lower-priority kernels, so the higher-priority kernel must wait for currently executing lower-priority blocks to finish).
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **Measured tail-latency impact.** The REEF paper (OSDI '22) reports that a real-time task's end-to-end latency was about 4 ms and stable alone, but its tail latency rose by over an order of magnitude, close to 50 ms, when run alongside best-effort tasks. REEF addresses this with microsecond-scale kernel preemption through reset-based preemption rather than relying on CUDA stream priorities.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **Interference quantified for DNN inference.** A 2025 scheduling paper measures kernel-execution interference reaching up to 151.66% at the 95th percentile when the maximum permitted batch concurrency is set to 2, and notes that the magnitude of interference may escalate as the concurrency level increases.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **Priority-aware serving systems.** Strait (arXiv 2604.28175) employs CUDA stream priorities and priority scheduling to favor high-priority tasks, treating low-priority tasks on a best-effort basis. It also models data-transfer and kernel-execution interference to improve latency estimates.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **Interference-aware provisioning.** iGniter (arXiv 2211.01713) studies co-located inference on a V100 and uses CUDA streams to overlap data loading with GPU execution. It also notes that kernels must be scheduled onto SMs, leading to a moderate amount of scheduling delay in the GPU execution stream.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  - **Adjacent work on embedded GPUs.** A study on shared last-level cache interference across multiple CUDA streams (arXiv 2310.04848) finds slowdowns from a concurrent memory-reading kernel and from concurrent host-to-device copies, though it targets embedded Tegra-class hardware.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  Overall, the sources agree that CUDA stream priorities give only partial isolation for latency-critical inference. Non-preemptive execution and shared memory-system contention still cause tail-latency spikes. The REEF and Strait papers are the most directly relevant to your query. I didn't find a single study that isolates stream priorities as the sole variable on current hardware, so you may need to check the full papers for their exact experimental setups.
  ⎿  
  ⎿

⏺ I added seven new PLAN items (M16–M22) that move translation and TTS onto the idle GPU. Each one cites the paper findings it rests on, collected in a new `RESEARCH.md` (10 findings). I read abstracts and search snippets, not full papers, so the paper numbers are the authors' own and still need confirming on our hardware.

**What the research says:**
- **Batch on the GPU:** systems like Nexus only pay off when many requests share each GPU call. A GPU TTS study served 100 requests/s on one A10 with first audio under 80 ms. Gains flatten past a batch of about 8.
- **Translation:** CTranslate2's own benchmark shows about 10× more tokens/s on GPU than on CPU int8. Orca-style batching lets clauses join and leave the batch at every decoding step.
- **Sharing hurts ASR unless it's protected:** CUDA stream priorities can't interrupt kernels already running. In the REEF paper, a 4 ms real-time task's worst cases reached about 50 ms when other work shared the GPU. Our ASR has a hard 160 ms deadline per chunk, so it must be protected.
- **Arena vs paged:** each stream's ASR state is a fixed 2.59 MB, so the memory fragmentation that paging solves in vLLM doesn't happen here. The decision is still yours.

**Local checks:**
- The Piper model accepts batches.
- The installed ONNX Runtime is CPU-only; it needs `onnxruntime-gpu`.
- Translation is int8, which ONNX Runtime's CUDA backend runs poorly, so it needs an fp16 export.

**New PLAN, in order:**
- **M16:** measure how much GPU headroom there really is.
- **M17:** translation on the GPU.
- **M18:** batched TTS on the GPU, with FastPitch as a fallback.
- **M19:** keep ASR on time when the GPU is shared, and re-test whether earliest-deadline-first beats first-come-first-served (SPEC hypothesis E4).
- **M20:** rerun capacity and cost. The hypothesis is 160+ users instead of 80; a miss gets reported as a finding.
- **M21 (🧑):** ASR speed-ups, only if ASR becomes the limit, plus your arena-vs-paged decision.
- **M22 (🧑):** a paid datacentre GPU run to replace my extrapolated numbers.

⏺ M16 is finished and committed (`9a84eae`), with the STATUS handoff in `f45ee8b`. At 80 users the GPU is mostly idle: busy 29% of the time (so at least 71% free), 35 W of its 70 W limit; TTS on the CPU is still the bottleneck. All tests pass.
- **Memory was the real limit:** the GPU had only 130 MiB free (6014 of 6144 MiB used) because PyTorch's allocator cache held 5.4 GB to serve a 1.2 GB peak. With `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True` usage drops to 1860 MiB, freeing 4.3 GB, with the same speed. M17 needs this setting before MT shares the GPU with ASR.
- **ASR time per 160 ms step:** the encoder takes 47 ms, about 90% of the GPU work. Computing the audio features takes 4.4 ms and the final decoding step 0.5 ms.
- **Added:** `bench/gpu_profile.py`, per-step timers in `worker/fc_engine.py`, and the `nvidia-ml-py` package (GPU monitoring) in the serve environment and `requirements/serve.txt`.

Should `expandable_segments` become the default for serving? I've proposed doing it as part of M17. Safe to clear; next is M17.
Turn 30#
what can be done then? shall we use a smaller model or something that sort?
Response (7 lines) — click to expand
⏺ No smaller model needed. ASR itself only uses 1.2 GB of GPU memory; the rest was PyTorch's cache, and one setting (`expandable_segments`) frees 4.3 GB at the same speed. A smaller model would cost accuracy and solve nothing.

The real limit is the CPU (TTS, then MT), while the GPU sits 71% idle. So the fix is to give the GPU more work: MT on GPU (M17), then TTS (M18), aiming for over 160 users from today's 80 (M20).

If ASR becomes the limit later, speed it up first with CUDA graphs (a GPU speed-up) or bf16 (half-precision numbers) (RESEARCH R7). A smaller model is the last resort.

I'd make `expandable_segments` the default and start M17 now. Go ahead?

⏺ M18 is blocked on a choice you need to make: TTS on the GPU works correctly but isn't fast enough, and with everything on the GPU at 80 users the run fails. Code and results are committed as WIP (`7700fcf`), M18 isn't ticked, and tests pass.
- **What works:** short requests are pooled and run 8 at a time on the GPU, and each clause's audio comes out exactly as long as when synthesized alone.
- **Throughput:** the GPU tops out at about 50 seconds of audio per second, while the 8-process CPU pool does about 87. First-piece p95 meets the 0.30 s target only up to about 4 simultaneous requests.
- **All on GPU at 80 users:** the GPU is 88% busy, first audio p95 reaches 13 s, and ASR misses 3.4% of its 160 ms deadlines (limit 1%).

Pick one:
- **A (my recommendation):** keep the CPU pool as main TTS and send only overflow or first pieces to the GPU, with a cap so ASR keeps its deadline.
- **B:** try a faster GPU voice: Piper compiled with TensorRT, or FastPitch (needs your licence check).
- **C:** record M18 as a negative result, keep TTS on the CPU, and go to M19.

⏺ I compared both options at 80 and 120 users. **B (TensorRT) is faster everywhere, so M18 now uses it** and is done (`79b771b`). B here means the Piper voice compiled with NVIDIA's TensorRT; FastPitch was left out because it needs your licence check.
- **How B works:** the light first half of the voice runs on the CPU, and the conv-heavy second half runs batched on TensorRT at half precision. With 32 simultaneous requests the first piece still arrives in 0.08 s (target ≤0.30 s), and throughput is about 9× the 8-process CPU pool.
- **80 users:** first audio p95 is 1.22 s with B vs 1.40 s with A (the hybrid).
- **120 users:** A fails (ASR misses 1.14% of its deadlines, first audio 1.71 s); B passes at 1.27 s with 0.16% misses. ASR is now the limiting stage.

All tests pass, including a new check that batched audio comes out exactly as long as unbatched. TensorRT (NVIDIA's free wheel) is now installed in the serve environment; its first engine build takes about 2.5 minutes, then it's cached. The live gateway nodes still use the CPU path; only the benchmarks use the GPU so far.

I saved your "update STATUS.md after every run" rule to memory, and STATUS.md is up to date. Next is M19, keeping the ASR deadline safe on the shared GPU. Safe to clear.

  ⎿  ## 1. Goal
  ⎿  Phone captures speech, sends only speech to a lab-GPU/cloud back end, gets spoken Hindi back with first audio ≤2.0 s p95. The phone stays thin: capture, VAD gate, Opus, WebSocket, playback. Target is a deployable pilot and a course project (viva, report, demo).
  ⎿  
  ⎿  ## 2. Architecture
  ⎿  phone ⇄ gateway ⇄ worker pool. Gateway: auth token, admission at ≤85% predicted load, sticky routing, 6 s Opus replay buffer, resume token. Worker: streaming ASR engine → clause segmenter → IndicTrans2 dist-200M int8 → Hindi TTS (CPU by default). Workers dial out to a small cloud gateway (labs open no port).

  ⎿  ## 3. Fixed facts and numbers
  ⎿  - Engine = repo GPU_Engine_ASR commit e5031d3 (RTX 3050 6 GB): FastConformer-114M, 160 ms chunks, attention [70,1], greedy CTC, 2.59 MB state/stream, slot-arena store.
  ⎿  - Engine capacity: 12 streams single, 112 batched (FCFS=EDF), 128 with VAD gate. s(1)=11 ms, s(32)=41 ms. WER 4.24% streaming vs 1.77% offline (283 words); gating does not hurt WER.
  ⎿  - Paging, CUDA graphs and GQA (384 streams, 448 with VAD) were measured on a random-weight 352 M model only. Never quote them as real-model results.
  ⎿  - The engine has NO shared silence page, NO session interface, NO text events or timestamps. The gate skips silent chunks. We add the rest.
  ⎿  - Capacity model: U=min(U_ASR, R_MT/(a·c), C/(a·g·r)); a=0.385, c=0.3 clauses/s, g=1.2, R_MT=20 clauses/s, r∈{0.1,0.2,0.4} core-s per audio-s. U_ASR≈250–290 (extrapolated).   ⎿  - Latency budget 1.25 s: 0.30 capture/gate/pack, 0.05 uplink, 0.35 ASR, 0.05 commit, 0.10 MT, 0.30 first speech piece, 0.10 downlink+jitter. Local on-phone baseline: 2.1 s first audio.

⏺ M19 is done and committed (1226acc, plus the STATUS update 8319081); its test passes at 130 users. The best fix was an EDF gate in `worker/gpu_share.py`: MT and TTS hold their GPU work while an ASR tick with an earlier deadline runs. It is now the default.
- **Results:** the gate cut ASR tick p95 by 6–8 ms at every load I tried. At 130 users that gives 0.099 s (FCFS 0.105 s), which meets the 0.10 s target. CUDA stream priorities and MPS made no difference, and moving MT/TTS to a separate process without MPS was much worse (34% of ticks missed).
- **E4 finding:** EDF does not equal FCFS on the shared GPU queue, so that hypothesis failed and is logged as a finding.
- **Limit:** above about 130 users, ASR on its own already misses the 0.10 s target (0.112 s at 160), so ASR is now the bottleneck.
- **Decision for you:** at 160 users the system still passes the SPEC test (first audio p95 1.57 s, 0.16% misses), so M20's capacity is either about 130 (tick target) or 160 or more (SPEC test). Which should count? It's in STATUS. Fast tests pass (68); safe to clear.

  ⎿  """C1 (D44): serve the pretrained cache-aware FastConformer-114M with the StreamServe engine. NeMo's own encoder
  ⎿  modules do the math (exact fidelity, no re-implementation); this module only owns the per-session state.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  Batch-uniform streaming = NeMo's pad_and_drop_preencoded mode: every chunk is [9 cached mel frames | 16 new frames]
  ⎿  (zeros before the first chunk) and the encoder drops its 2 extra pre-encoded frames, so all sessions in a batch
  ⎿  have the same shapes regardless of where they are in their stream. Per-session state (slot arena, D27-style):

- **RAM:** while streaming for 90 s, memory use (PSS) had a median of 83.1 MB and a peak of 87.5 MB. Your budget is 250 MB (`results/android_mem.csv`).

⏺ Here are the commands. I couldn't find a record of the earlier tunnel (the old VoiceAI phone setup ran straight off the laptop with `adb reverse`), so this setup is new and untested. The phone plugs into the Windows laptop by USB, and one SSH session carries two forwards. The first, `-R 5037`, lets the adb on this Linux machine (10.81.30.62) drive the phone. The second, `-L 8765`, lets the phone reach the gateway on this machine.

**Windows (PowerShell, phone on USB with USB debugging on, Android platform-tools installed):**
```
adb start-server ; adb devices
ssh -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -R 5037:127.0.0.1:5037 -L 8765:127.0.0.1:8765 krishnag@10.81.30.62
```
**Linux (run inside that SSH session):**
```
adb kill-server ; adb devices
cd ~/VoiceMesh/Voicemesh && .venv/bin/python -m gateway.launch --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8765
```
The first line stops the local adb server so `adb` uses the laptop's through the tunnel; `adb devices` should then list your phone. The second line starts the gateway; leave it running.

**Linux (a second SSH terminal):**
```
adb reverse tcp:8765 tcp:8765
```
After that, set the URL in the app to `ws://127.0.0.1:8765` (its default `10.0.2.2` only works on the emulator).

Two things can break it:
- **Phone reconnects:** `adb reverse` is cleared every time, so re-run it.
- **adb versions differ:** this machine has adb 1.0.41. If the laptop's adb version differs, the Linux side may restart its own server, so keep the versions matching.

⏺ I've read the Android part of VoiceAI. I'm reading your 100 MB target as the phone's RAM (now 142 MB). VoiceAI's GPU and kernel work only changes server cost, not phone RAM. The app's one model is the Silero speech detector, and the ONNX Runtime library it runs on is most of the app. From VoiceAI, these are the ways to cut, biggest first; the savings are my estimates and none are measured yet:
1. **Remove ONNX Runtime (biggest win):** VoiceAI hand-wrote a fast int8 conv kernel (H-D2/H-D3). The same approach could run the speech detector's small model in a few hundred lines of native code, or use a cut-down runtime with only the operations it needs. This drops a 33 MB library, maybe 15–30 MB of RAM.
2. **Measure a release build:** the 142 MB was from a debug build, and release builds usually use less memory.
3. **Shrink the app code:** turning on minification (it's off here, as it was in VoiceAI, Z-D1) cuts the code size, saving a few MB.
4. **Thread count:** already done; the speech detector uses one thread, matching VoiceAI's thread lesson (A-D16).

⏺ VoiceAI used four kinds of optimization, and most of them carry over to VoiceMesh. All the numbers in the "Use in VoiceMesh" table are my estimates; none are measured yet.

**What VoiceAI did:**
1. **Measure before changing anything:** it profiled each operation on the phone, then used CPU profiling and disassembly (`simpleperf`) and a hardware-limit (roofline) model. That showed 42% of speech-synthesis (TTS) time was slow byte loops and 21–27% was threads spinning while waiting.
2. **Custom kernels:** a hand-written int8 conv kernel using the phone CPU's fast dot-product instructions, plugged into ONNX Runtime. That made the Piper voice 2.64× faster with identical audio. Packing only one weight layout saved 36 MB of RAM.
3. **Runtime and system tuning:** threads limited to the fast cores (17–22% faster), models loaded in parallel (start-up 10 s → 3.6 s), and one copy of ONNX Runtime instead of two (APK 32.9 → 23.1 MB).
4. **Size cuts:** compressed native libraries, 68.7 MB of dead model weights removed, and a plan for minification, a cut-down ONNX Runtime, 4-bit weights and a Hindi-only vocabulary.

**Use in VoiceMesh, phone side:**

| Change | Saves | Effort |
|---|---|---|
| Turn off ONNX Runtime's memory arena and memory-pattern caching for the speech detector (M14 found that caching grows memory on the server) | ~5–10 MB RAM | One line, low risk |
| Build ONNX Runtime with only the speech detector's operations (VoiceAI's Z3 plan) | ~15 MB RAM, ~20 MB disk | Half a day to a day |
| Or replace ONNX Runtime with a native speech-detector kernel (VoiceAI's H2 approach; the model is tiny) | ~20–25 MB RAM, ~30 MB disk | 1–2 days, must give the same decisions |
| Turn on R8 minification and build a release APK for arm64 only | APK 35 → ~15 MB, a few MB RAM | Small |
| Stream with the screen off or app in the background (already measured) | ~47 MB | None |

Together that brings streaming down from 100 MB to an estimated **~70–80 MB**, and the installed size to **~15–25 MB**.

**Server side (cost per user):** VoiceAI's Hindi vocabulary shortlist (122k → ~25–30k words, about 60 MB less read per token) and 4-bit weights both apply to the IndicTrans2 translation model on the 3050. Its int8 conv kernel would help the CPU speech-synthesis stack (the 80-user limit) only after porting to x86.

I'd start with the one-line arena change plus the release/arm64/minified build, which are cheap and safe. Then I'd do the cut-down ONNX Runtime. Shall I go ahead?

⏺ The release build is done and runs on your phone. Streaming uses **72 MB** of RAM, well under your ~100 MB target, but the arena change didn't help.

| | Debug (before) | Release (now) |
|---|---|---|
| APK size | 35.3 MB | 14.8 MB |
| RAM while streaming, app in background, screen off | 100.3 MB | 72.0 MB |

- **Arena change:** native memory stayed at about 32 MB. I kept it since it does no harm.
- **Where the release saving came from:** Java memory fell from 14 to 3.5 MB, system from 16.6 to 6.4 MB, and code from 29 to 23 MB.
- **Screen buffers:** turning the screen off alone doesn't always free them; one run kept 51.5 MB of graphics. Sending the app to the home screen does free them.
- **Room was quiet:** the speech detector sent nothing to the server, so these runs don't include sending or playing audio.

To let the release build reach the lab over `adb reverse`, it now allows unencrypted `ws://` only to `127.0.0.1`/`localhost`; everything else needs TLS. The debug build still allows `ws://` to any address. The release is signed with the debug key and is only for local testing; a real signing key is still to do. It's installed on the phone now, so the URL and token have to be typed in the app.

STATUS.md and INSIGHTS.md are updated, and nothing is committed yet. Next would be slimming or removing ONNX Runtime, which is most of the remaining 31 MB of native memory.

⏺ I found nothing blocking for tomorrow's RTX 3050 demo. All tests pass, the report check is clean, and DEMO §1 (English in, Hindi out, `pass_g1=True`) and §2 (node kill, `pass=True`) both ran fine. Afterwards I put `results/` and the report back to the committed numbers.
- I also ran the phone setup (gateway plus the all-GPU worker) with 2 simulated phones on this PC and both got Hindi audio back. The worker starts in about 12 s and uses about 3.5 GB of the 6 GB card. The phone wasn't touched.
- I fixed the open bug where a VAD error crashed the app; now it just stops streaming (commit `d0e7563`). The release APK builds and unit tests pass, but it hasn't been checked on the phone yet.
- For questions: §1 shows a negative p50 (`-1.73 s`). This is expected, because the first Hindi clause plays before the speaker finishes (INSIGHTS.md has the note). Also call the demo "research", since the Piper voice licences aren't cleared.
- I didn't re-run §3 (emulator). Tell me when the phone is free and I'll do the speak test.

  ⎿   * so the first syllable is not clipped. Sequence numbers are time slots; gaps mean silence.
  ⎿   */
  ⎿  class Gate<T>(
  ⎿      private val threshold: Float = 0.5f,
  ⎿      private val hangover: Int = 3,

  ⎿      /** Feeds chunk [seq] with its max speech probability; returns chunks to send now, oldest first. */
  ⎿      fun push(seq: Int, chunk: T, prob: Float): List<Pair<Int, T>> {

⏺ The phone tests pass with the new UI. Testing turned up two crashes in my UI change, and both are fixed and committed (`4cfc340`).
- **Speak test:** passed on the small release build. The voice detector let speech through, the server built 3 clauses, and the phone played 4 Hindi clips. Light and dark mode both look right, and an expired token now shows "Server refused" and stops cleanly.
- **Crashes fixed:**
  - The app crashed on launch on Android 15.
  - Tapping STOP closed the whole app.
  - The constantly refreshing screen also blocked `uiautomator` dumps, which tap automation depends on; that's fixed too.
- **Memory:** about 80 MB while streaming in the background. I measured the build from before the UI change under the same conditions today and it was about 82 MB, so the UI didn't add anything. Neither build matches the 63.7 MB measured on 10-21.
- **Still untested on the phone:** the earlier fix for a crash when the voice detector fails, because I can't make that failure happen on purpose yet.

  ⎿  # SPEC.md: VoiceMesh Go (live English→Hindi voice translation for 2 GB Android Go phones)
  ⎿  Source of truth. Do not change the stack (§4) or numbers (§3) without asking the user.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  ## 0. Token rules (obey always)
  ⎿  1. Session start: read STATUS.md only (≤30 lines), then only the SPEC section it names.
  ⎿  2. Never read big files (logs, CSVs, models, reports). Use grep, `head -n 40`, `tail -n 40`, `wc -l`, or a Python one-liner that prints summary numbers.
  ⎿  3. Targeted Edit calls only; never rewrite a whole file except STATUS.md. No subagents. No web search unless the task says so.
  ⎿  4. Replies ≤5 lines. Pipe tool output through head/tail. Run tests with `-q` and show failures only.
  ⎿  5. One task per session: take the first unticked PLAN.md item, finish, test, commit, update STATUS.md, stop.
  ⎿  6. After every commit rewrite STATUS.md (§6). The user may `/clear` at any time; STATUS.md alone must be enough to continue.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  ## 1. Goal
  ⎿  Phone captures speech, sends only speech to a lab-GPU/cloud back end, gets spoken Hindi back with first audio ≤2.0 s p95. The phone stays thin: capture, VAD gate, Opus, WebSocket, playback. Target is a deployable pilot and a course project (viva, report, demo).
  ⎿  
  ⎿  ## 2. Architecture
  ⎿  phone ⇄ gateway ⇄ worker pool. Gateway: auth token, admission at ≤85% predicted load, sticky routing, 6 s Opus replay buffer, resume token. Worker: streaming ASR engine → clause segmenter → IndicTrans2 dist-200M int8 → Hindi TTS (CPU by default). Workers dial out to a small cloud gateway (labs open no port).
  ⎿  
  ⎿  ## 3. Fixed facts and numbers
  ⎿  - Engine = repo GPU_Engine_ASR commit e5031d3 (RTX 3050 6 GB): FastConformer-114M, 160 ms chunks, attention [70,1], greedy CTC, 2.59 MB state/stream, slot-arena store.
  ⎿  - Engine capacity: 12 streams single, 112 batched (FCFS=EDF), 128 with VAD gate. s(1)=11 ms, s(32)=41 ms. WER 4.24% streaming vs 1.77% offline (283 words); gating does not hurt WER.
  ⎿  - Paging, CUDA graphs and GQA (384 streams, 448 with VAD) were measured on a random-weight 352 M model only. Never quote them as real-model results.
  ⎿  - The engine has NO shared silence page, NO session interface, NO text events or timestamps. The gate skips silent chunks. We add the rest.
  ⎿  - Capacity model: U=min(U_ASR, R_MT/(a·c), C/(a·g·r)); a=0.385, c=0.3 clauses/s, g=1.2, R_MT=20 clauses/s, r∈{0.1,0.2,0.4} core-s per audio-s. U_ASR≈250–290 (extrapolated). TTS limits first: lab PC 8 cores ≈87 users, cloud T4 4 vCPU ≈43. Measured (M7, idle): lab passes 70 users (p95 1.86 s), fails 75–85; 70 is the lab capacity. M15 (TTS rate 1.15): passes 80 (3/3, p95 1.74 s), 75 3/4, fails 85 (2.19 s); 80 is the lab capacity.
  ⎿  - Cost per user-hour: lab 0.001–0.0025 USD, cloud 0.014–0.061 USD. Measured (M7, 70 users): lab 0.0037 incl. cloud-gateway egress, T4 0.016 on-demand / 0.0062 spot.
  ⎿  - Latency budget 1.25 s: 0.30 capture/gate/pack, 0.05 uplink, 0.35 ASR, 0.05 commit, 0.10 MT, 0.30 first speech piece, 0.10 downlink+jitter. Local on-phone baseline: 2.1 s first audio.
  ⎿  - Licences: IndicTrans2 MIT, Silero MIT, sherpa-onnx Apache-2.0. Piper pratham/priyamvada are CC-BY-NC-SA (not for sale); `rohan` unverified; Android system Hindi voice is the commercial fallback. FastConformer licence text unread.
  ⎿  
  ⎿  ## 4. Stack (defaults; log any deviation in INSIGHTS.md)
  ⎿  Client Kotlin: AudioRecord 16 kHz mono, Silero VAD (ONNX) with hangover and pre-roll, Opus ~16 kbit/s, OkHttp WebSocket, jitter buffer, AudioTrack, foreground service. Server Python 3.12 asyncio. Engine, MT and TTS run in worker processes. Tests: pytest (fast = `-m "not slow"`), Gradle unit tests. Lint: ruff.

  ⎿          self._rs = av.AudioResampler(format="s16", layout="mono", rate=OPUS_RATE)
  ⎿          self._buf = np.zeros(0, np.int16)
  ⎿          self._av = av

Turn 80#
what are the cases when tunnel can restart?
Response (10 lines) — click to expand
⏺ The public URL changes only when the `cloudflared` process itself restarts. That happens when:

1. **The PC reboots or loses power.** The services come back on their own, but the tunnel gets a new URL.
2. **`cloudflared` crashes or is killed**, for example by the system running out of memory. systemd restarts it within 10 s, with a new URL.
3. **Someone restarts it by hand**, with `systemctl --user restart voicemesh-tunnel` or by re-running the install command in `deploy/README.md`.
4. **Cloudflare drops the tunnel on its side.** Quick tunnels are meant for testing and come with no uptime guarantee.

These don't change the URL: a Wi-Fi or network drop (it reconnects with the same URL), restarting the gateway, worker or web service, logging out, or self-updates (I turned those off).

To protect the submission, I can set up a check that alerts you if the URL changes, or move to a fixed URL (this needs a free ngrok or Cloudflare account from you).

⏺ The way to do it on Windows is WSL2, which runs Ubuntu inside Windows and can use your laptop's GPU through the normal Windows NVIDIA driver. The worker has only been tested on Linux, so this is the safest route. Steps:

```
1. PowerShell (Admin):  wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04   → reboot, open "Ubuntu"
2. Ubuntu: nvidia-smi   (should show the 3050; don't install a Linux NVIDIA driver, Windows provides it)
3. Ubuntu: sudo apt install -y python3.12-venv rsync && mkdir ~/VoiceMesh && cd ~/VoiceMesh
   rsync -a --exclude out --exclude results krishnag@10.81.30.62:VoiceMesh/{Voicemesh,GPU_Engine_ASR,models} .
   python3.12 -m venv .venv_serve && .venv_serve/bin/pip install -r Voicemesh/requirements/serve.txt
4. Ubuntu, leave open: ssh -N -L 8765:127.0.0.1:8765 krishnag@10.81.30.62
5. Ubuntu, new tab: cd ~/VoiceMesh/Voicemesh && VM_SECRET=<value from lab ~/.config/voicemesh/env> \
   ../.venv_serve/bin/python -m worker.pipeline --url ws://127.0.0.1:8765 --id laptop1
```

Step 3 downloads about 12 GB, mostly CUDA torch. The worker needs the same `VM_SECRET` as the lab gateway or it will be refused, so copy it from the lab machine rather than using the default.

Once step 5 is running, the laptop joins as a second node. After your 14:00 submission I can stop the lab worker so all traffic goes to your GPU; I've noted this plan in STATUS.md.

⏺ Probably yes, but it's untested on Windows. I checked the code the worker actually runs:

- **No Triton needed:** the real speech-recognition engine path uses plain torch. Triton is only used by the test-model code, so CUDA graphs and fp16 should still work. Windows signal handling is only needed by the gateway, which stays on the lab PC.
- **What blocks it:** `requirements/serve.txt` pins packages that only install on Linux (`triton`, `nvidia-nccl`, `nvidia-cufile`, `nvidia-nvshmem`). Marking them Linux-only would fix that without changing anything on Linux.
- **Main risk:** NeMo (the speech toolkit the engine loads its model with) doesn't officially support Windows. Loading the model may need a fix, and I can't test that from the lab machine.

Should I make that requirements change and write a `laptop_worker.ps1` launcher (venv, SSH tunnel, worker)? WSL2 remains the safer option before today's 14:00 deadline. I've added this to STATUS.md.

  ⎿  
  ⎿  Batch-uniform streaming = NeMo's pad_and_drop_preencoded mode: every chunk is [9 cached mel frames | 16 new frames]
  ⎿  (zeros before the first chunk) and the encoder drops its 2 extra pre-encoded frames, so all sessions in a batch

⏺ I've fixed the error; you need to re-download the script and run setup again. Exit 141 meant the laptop stopped reading the download partway through, most likely because Windows `ssh` doesn't handle a large stream redirected through `cmd` well.

Setup no longer streams anything. The lab PC writes the bundle to a file, your laptop copies it with `scp`, and then the copy on the lab is deleted. It also now checks free disk space first, because setup needs about 9 GB. I tested the bundle step on the lab, but the Windows side is still untested.
